"Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) or government-owned companies incorporated under the Companies Act, such as ONGC or NTPC, which are treated as 'companies' under the Act and not as 'Departments of Government'."

Does this fall within 'Department of Government' under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986?

I, Inspector Rajesh Kumar, Labour Enforcement Officer, District Labour Office, Firozabad, conducted a surprise inspection on 15th March 2024 at M/s Shivam Glass Bangle Factory, Shikohabad Road, Firozabad. During inspection, I found 12 children aged between 9-14 years working in the furnace section where temperature exceeded 45°C. The children were engaged in glass melting and bangle polishing work involving exposure to molten glass, silica dust, and sharp tools. Medical examination revealed burns on hands of 4 children. Factory owner Mukesh Agarwal, son of Ram Prakash Agarwal, resident of Nehru Colony, Firozabad, admitted employing these children for 10-12 hours daily at Rs. 150-200 per day. No safety equipment provided. Children identified as Ravi (age 11), Sonu (age 10), Guddu (age 13), and others were working in hazardous conditions prohibited under Schedule of Child and Adolescent Labour Act. The employer also maintained false attendance records showing adult workers. Factory premises lacked basic ventilation and fire safety measures. This constitutes gross violation of child labour laws endangering life and health of minors.

I, Constable Rajesh Kumar, stationed at Sadar Police Station, Meerut, hereby report that on 15th March 2024, based on credible intelligence, a raid was conducted at House No. 47, Shastri Nagar, Meerut. During the raid, accused Vikram Singh was apprehended. Upon interrogation, Vikram Singh confessed that he had been instigated by accused Mohit Verma to commit theft at the residence of Shri Anil Kapoor located at B-12, Civil Lines, Meerut. Mohit Verma had provided detailed information about the layout of the house, timings when the house would be empty, and also supplied duplicate keys to facilitate the theft. On 10th March 2024, Vikram Singh entered the house using the keys provided by Mohit Verma and stole gold jewellery worth Rs. 2,50,000, cash amounting to Rs. 75,000, and one laptop valued at Rs. 60,000. The stolen property was handed over to Mohit Verma who sold the items and shared the proceeds equally with Vikram Singh. Furthermore, Mohit Verma had promised to pay Vikram Singh an additional Rs. 50,000 for undertaking the risk. Mohit Verma also intentionally harboured Vikram Singh at his residence at Flat No. 203, Green Park Apartments, Meerut, for three days after the theft to help him evade arrest. Both accused persons are being arrested and further investigation is underway.

I, Kavita Sharma, W/o Rajesh Sharma, aged 32 years, R/o House No. 47, Sector 12, Rohini, Delhi, hereby lodge this complaint against my husband Rajesh Sharma and my mother-in-law Sunita Sharma. Since our marriage on 15th February 2019, they have been subjecting me to continuous mental torture and harassment. My husband constantly abuses me with filthy language, calling me 'useless', 'barren woman', and 'burden on family' in front of relatives and neighbours. He threatens me daily saying 'I will throw you out of this house' and 'You will die here, no one will help you'. My mother-in-law also taunts me every day, saying 'You cannot even cook properly' and 'We wasted money on your marriage'. On 10th March 2024, my husband slapped me twice on my face during an argument over household expenses, causing swelling on my left cheek. Since January 2024, my husband has stopped giving me any money for household expenses or my personal needs, forcing me to borrow from my parents. On 25th March 2024 at around 9 PM, when I asked for money to buy groceries, he grabbed my gold mangalsutra weighing approximately 15 grams worth Rs. 85,000 and snatched it from my neck, saying 'This belongs to my family now'. He also took my mobile phone Samsung Galaxy M31 worth Rs. 18,000 and refused to return it. Yesterday on 28th March 2024, he again threatened me saying 'If you don't leave this house, I will kill you and no one will find your body'. I am living in constant fear and mental agony. I request appropriate legal action.

What is expressly NOT covered by the term 'illegal omission' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?

'illegal omission' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 does NOT cover:
- A mere failure to act that is not backed by any legal obligation to act — for example, a bystander who has no legal duty to rescue a drowning person and does not attempt to do so.
- An omission arising from incapacity, accident, or genuine ignorance, where there is no criminal knowledge or intention, and no legal duty was imposed on the person to act.
- A failure to perform a moral or social duty that is not legally mandated, such as a neighbour failing to help during a domestic dispute when not bound by law to intervene.
- Omissions that fall within the General Exceptions of the Sanhita, such as an act or omission done by a child under seven years of age.

Under the Code on Wages, 2019 / Labour Codes, what does 'casual worker' mean?

In plain terms: A casual worker is someone hired on a day-to-day basis and paid daily, without any long-term commitment from the employer. Their work with the same employer must not stretch beyond 14 consecutive working days. Once that limit is crossed, the worker may no longer be considered 'casual' under the law. Legally: A person engaged by the day and from day to day who is paid on a daily basis and whose engagement by one and the same employer does not exceed 14 consecutive working days customary in the business in which the worker is engaged. (Source: Code on Wages, 2019 / Labour Codes, Section 2.)

Define the term 'bailable' as used in the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015.

In plain terms: A 'bailable' offence is one where a person accused of a crime has the legal right to be released on bail — the police or court cannot refuse bail as a matter of discretion. Under the Juvenile Justice Act, offences that carry a punishment of less than three years in prison or only a fine fall into this category. It means the accused does not have to wait for a judge to decide whether bail will be granted; it is granted automatically upon request with or without a surety. Legally: An offence under the Juvenile Justice Act is bailable where it is punishable with imprisonment for less than three years or with fine only, in which case the accused has a right to be released on bail as a matter of course. Such offences are also non-cognizable under Section 86 of the Act. (Source: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, Section 86.)

Define the term 'assault' as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

In plain terms: Assault means making a threatening gesture or action that causes another person to reasonably fear that they are about to be physically harmed. The threat must be communicated through a gesture or physical preparation — words alone are not enough. However, words spoken alongside a threatening gesture can make that gesture count as an assault. Legally: A person is said to commit 'assault' when he makes any gesture or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person. Explanation: Mere words do not amount to an assault; but the words which a person uses may give to his gestures or preparations such a meaning as may make those gestures or preparations amount to an assault. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 130.)

Why is the legal definition of 'non-testamentary instrument' important under the Registration Act, 1908?

Whether a document qualifies as a non-testamentary instrument directly determines whether it attracts compulsory registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908; failure to register a compulsorily registrable non-testamentary instrument renders it inadmissible as evidence of the transaction it purports to effect and unenforceable in a court of law. It also determines the applicability of Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, for part-performance of contracts, which requires the underlying document to be a registered non-testamentary instrument.

What is meant by 'good faith' in Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, Section 100?

In plain terms: Good faith means acting honestly and sincerely, without any hidden bad motive or intention to harm, while carrying out duties under the Juvenile Justice Act. If a government official or any person acting under government directions does something incorrectly but genuinely believed they were doing the right thing under the law, they are protected from being sued or prosecuted. It is about the intent behind the action, not whether the action was ultimately correct or beneficial. Legally: Good faith, as used in Section 100 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, refers to any act done or intended to be done honestly and sincerely in pursuance of the Act or any rules or regulations made thereunder, without malice or fraudulent intent, even if such act results in error or causes harm. The Act does not provide a formal definition but extends protection from suit, prosecution or other legal proceedings to the Central Government, State Government, or any person acting under their directions in respect of anything done in good faith. (Source: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, Section 100.)

Define the term 'conspiracy' as used in the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012.

In plain terms: Conspiracy means when two or more people plan or agree together to commit a sexual offence against a child under this law, and then at least one actual step or wrongful act is taken to carry out that plan. It does not matter if the main offence is ultimately completed — the planning and the step taken together are enough. Any person who was part of the agreement can be held responsible even if they did not personally commit the final act. Legally: Conspiracy, as used under the Act, refers to an agreement or engagement between two or more persons for the doing of an offence under this Act, where an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that agreement and in order to the doing of that offence. It forms the second limb of abetment under Section 16, and an act or offence is committed in consequence of such conspiracy when it is carried out in pursuance of the conspiratorial agreement. (Source: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, Section 16.)

What is meant by 'quarantine' in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 273?

In plain terms: Quarantine is a government-imposed restriction that keeps a vehicle, ship, aircraft, or other mode of transport — or a place — isolated or under controlled conditions to stop the spread of a dangerous infectious disease. During quarantine, movement to and from affected areas is regulated by official government rules. Anyone who knowingly breaks these rules can be punished under this law. Legally: Quarantine, as used in Section 273 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the state of isolation or restricted intercourse imposed by the Government upon any mode of transport or place for the purpose of preventing the spread of infectious disease, governed by rules made by the Government regulating the movement of such transport and the intercourse between places where an infectious disease prevails and other places. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 273.)

Under the Registration Act, 1908, what does 'Book No. 2' mean?

In plain terms: Book No. 2 is a specific official record book maintained at every registration office where the registering officer writes down the reasons whenever they refuse to register a document. Think of it as a 'rejection log' — if your property sale deed or any other document is refused registration, the officer must write the exact reasons in this book. Anyone whose document was refused can ask for a free copy of those reasons from this book. Legally: Book No. 2 is the official register maintained by Sub-Registrars and Registrars in which orders of refusal to register a document are recorded, along with the reasons for such refusal, as required under Sections 71 and 76 of the Registration Act. It serves as the formal record of all refusals to register documents, distinct from the registers maintained for documents that are accepted for registration. (Source: Registration Act, 1908, Section 71.)

What is expressly NOT covered by the term 'contract of service' under the Copyright Act, 1957?

'contract of service' under the Copyright Act, 1957 does NOT cover:
- Freelancers or independent contractors engaged for a specific project without an ongoing employer-employee relationship, as they operate under a contract for service, not a contract of service.
- Authors who create works on their own initiative, outside of their employment duties and without direction from an employer, even if they happen to be employed elsewhere.
- Persons engaged under apprenticeship agreements, which are treated separately and distinctly from contracts of service in the proviso to Section 17.
- Works commissioned from an external creator (such as a portrait or photograph) at the instance of a person, which fall under a separate clause in Section 17 governing commissioned works.

Define the term 'Schedule' as used in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

In plain terms: The Schedule is an official list or table attached at the end of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which contains important details or categories that the Act refers to. It works like an appendix that is legally binding, just like the main text of the law. The government has the power to update or modify this Schedule through an official notification without passing an entirely new law. Legally: The Schedule, as used in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, refers to the formal annexure appended to the Act containing specified lists, particulars, or enumerations that form an integral part of the Act, having the same legal force as the body of the Act itself. Under the Copyright Act, 1957, what does 'pseudonymous work' mean?

In plain terms: A pseudonymous work is one where the author publishes under a fake or pen name rather than their real name, so the true identity of the creator is hidden from the public. Copyright in such a work lasts for 60 years from the year it was first published, but if the author's real identity becomes known before that period ends, the copyright then lasts for 60 years after the author's death. The publisher of such a work can act as the copyright owner until the real author's identity is publicly revealed. Legally: A pseudonymous work is a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work published under a name that is not the true identity of the author, i.e., under a fictitious or assumed name. For such a work, copyright subsists until sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year next following the year of first publication, unless the author's true identity is disclosed before expiry of that period, in which case copyright subsists for sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year next following the year of the author's death. (Source: Copyright Act, 1957, Section 23.)

Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, what does 'conspiracy' mean?

In plain terms: A conspiracy is when two or more people agree together to do something illegal or to cause something illegal to happen. For a conspiracy to count as abetment, at least one actual step — an action or a deliberate failure to act — must be taken by someone to carry out that plan. Importantly, every member of the conspiracy can be held responsible even if they did not personally meet or directly coordinate with the person who ultimately committed the act. Legally: A conspiracy for the purposes of abetment exists when a person engages with one or more other persons in an agreement for the doing of a thing, provided that an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy and in order to the doing of that thing. It is not necessary that the abettor should concert the offence with the person who commits it; it is sufficient if he engages in the conspiracy in pursuance of which the offence is committed. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 45.)

In plain terms: A tractor is a type of motor vehicle recognised under the Motor Vehicles Act as a separate category, distinct from cars, motorcycles, goods carriages, and road-rollers. Legally: "tractor" is not separately defined in the Act but is referenced in the definitions of 'heavy goods vehicle' and 'light motor vehicle' as a distinct category of motor vehicle whose unladen weight determines its classification — specifically, a tractor the unladen weight of which does not exceed 7500 kilograms is a light motor vehicle, and a tractor the unladen weight of which exceeds 12,000 kilograms falls within the definition of heavy goods vehicle. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, what does 'direction of law' mean?

In plain terms: A 'direction of law' is basically a clear instruction given by a law that tells a person — especially a government official or someone holding a position of trust — exactly how they must do their job or handle property. It is not just a general duty but a specific rule about the way something must be done. If a person knowingly ignores this instruction, especially to harm someone or help someone escape punishment, they can be held criminally liable. Legally: A 'direction of law' refers to any statutory mandate, rule, or legal provision that prescribes the specific manner, mode, or conduct in which a public servant or a person entrusted with property or duty is required to act or perform their functions. It encompasses any legally imposed obligation governing the way an act is to be carried out, including directions found in statutes, codes, court orders, or regulations that have the force of law. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 198.)

In plain terms: The 'State Government' means the elected government of a particular Indian State, responsible for making and enforcing road transport rules within that State. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, what does 'escape' mean?

In plain terms: Escape means when a State prisoner or prisoner of war leaves the place or limits where they are legally held or permitted to stay, without permission. This includes not just physically breaking out of a prison, but also when a prisoner on parole goes beyond the geographical boundaries set for them. Essentially, any unauthorised departure from the place or limits of lawful custody counts as an escape. Legally: A State prisoner or prisoner of war is said to escape from lawful custody if such prisoner goes beyond the limits within which he is allowed to be at large, including where a prisoner permitted to be at large on parole within certain limits in India goes beyond those limits. More broadly, 'escape' encompasses any act by which a State prisoner or prisoner of war leaves or is removed from lawful custody without authorisation. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 158.)

What is expressly NOT covered by the term 'effective licence' under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988?

'effective licence' under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 does NOT cover:
- A conductor's licence that has passed its expiry date without renewal, even if the physical document is still in the holder's possession.
- A conductor's licence that has been suspended by the licensing authority or a court, as it ceases to be effective during the period of suspension.

- An application for a conductor's licence that is pending approval — a mere application does not constitute an effective licence.

Under the Arms Act, 1959, what does 'identification mark' mean?

In plain terms: An identification mark is any name, serial number, or other marking that a manufacturer places on a gun or ammunition to show who made it and to uniquely identify that particular weapon. Think of it like a vehicle's chassis number or a product's serial number — it links the firearm back to its maker and allows authorities to track it. The government decides the approved format and placement of these marks. Legally: An identification mark, in relation to a firearm or ammunition, means any name, number or other mark stamped or otherwise shown on a firearm or ammunition in a manner approved by the Central Government, including the name of the maker and the manufacturer's number, which serves to identify the origin and authenticity of the weapon or ammunition. (Source: Arms Act, 1959, Section 8.)

Define the term 'accrued benefits' as used in the Code on Wages, 2019 / Labour Codes.

In plain terms: Accrued benefits are all the payments and entitlements an employee has earned during their time working but has not yet received by the time their employment ends. This includes things like unpaid wages, unused leave pay, bonuses already earned, and any other dues that have built up over the course of the job. The employer must pay all of these in full on the last day of employment. Legally: Accrued benefits means all entitlements and remuneration that have been earned or accumulated by an employee during the course of employment under a contract of employment, which remain due and payable to the employee upon the termination or completion of that contract. Such benefits include all monetary and non-monetary entitlements that have vested or become owing by virtue of the employee's service, irrespective of whether they have been formally demanded or claimed. (Source: Code on Wages, 2019 / Labour Codes, Section 125.)

Define the term 'criminal conspiracy' as used in the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985.

In plain terms: A criminal conspiracy under the NDPS Act means when two or more people plan or agree together to commit a drug-related crime, even if the crime never actually happens. You can be punished just for being part of the plan. This includes conspiracies hatched in India to commit drug offences abroad, and also covers repeat offenders who face much harsher sentences for conspiring again after a prior conviction. Legally: A criminal conspiracy, within the meaning of the NDPS Act, means an agreement between two or more persons to commit an offence punishable under Chapter IV of the Act, and includes an agreement, made in India, to commit an act outside India that would either constitute such an offence if committed within India or constitutes an offence relating to narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances under the laws of that place with analogous legal conditions. What is meant by 'admission' in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 242?

In plain terms: An admission, in this context, is when someone pretending to be another person makes a statement or acknowledges something as true during a legal case or court proceeding. This could be saying something that admits guilt, accepts a claim, or concedes a legal point on behalf of the person being impersonated. The danger is that such a false admission can seriously harm the rights and legal standing of the real person whose identity was stolen. Legally: An 'admission' under Section 242 refers to any statement, acknowledgment, or concession made by a person who has falsely assumed the identity of another individual within the context of a suit or criminal prosecution, whereby such person makes a declaration or acknowledgment of facts that may affect the rights or liabilities of the person being impersonated. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 242.)

Why is the legal definition of 'slavery' important under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?

Whether a kidnapping or abduction is committed with intent to subject the victim to slavery determines the severity of punishment under Section 140, elevating the offence to one attracting imprisonment of either description for up to ten years along with fine. Establishing that the accused intended or knew the victim would be subjected to slavery is a key element that distinguishes this aggravated form of abduction from lesser offences of wrongful confinement or ordinary kidnapping.

Why is the legal definition of 'voluntary collective agreement' important under the Code on Wages, 2019 / Labour Codes?

Under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, what does 'person' mean?

In plain terms: A 'person' under this law is not limited to a human being. It covers a wide range of entities — from individual humans to families, companies, firms, clubs, trusts, and even foreign branches or offices controlled by any of these entities. Essentially, anyone or any organisation that can hold property, conduct transactions, or be held legally responsible can qualify as a 'person' under this Act. Legally: 'Person' includes an individual, a Hindu undivided family, a company, a firm, an association of persons or a body of individuals, whether incorporated or not, every artificial juridical person not falling within any of the preceding sub-clauses, and any agency, office or branch owned or controlled by any of the above persons mentioned in the preceding sub-clauses. (Source: Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, Section 2.)

Define the term 'dangerous driving' as used in the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.

In plain terms: Dangerous driving means operating a motor vehicle in a way that poses a serious risk of harm or death to people around it — whether on a road, highway, or any public place. It is not just careless or negligent driving; the manner of driving must be so unsafe that it could reasonably be expected to kill or seriously injure someone. The law considers the road conditions, traffic, and the type of vehicle involved when deciding if driving was dangerous. Legally: Dangerous driving, as used in the Motor Vehicles Act with reference to section 184, means the driving of a motor vehicle of any class or description in a manner which is dangerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the case, including the nature, condition, and use of the place where the vehicle is driven and the amount of traffic which actually is at the time, or which might reasonably be expected to be, at that place, resulting in or capable of resulting in the death of, or grievous hurt to, one or more persons. (Source: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, Section 21.)

What is expressly NOT covered by the term 'mistake of fact' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?

'mistake of fact' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 does NOT cover:
- A mistake about the law itself — i.e., a person's wrong belief that a particular law permits a certain act, or ignorance of what the law provides — does not qualify as a mistake of fact and does not provide a defence.
- Beliefs that are not held in good faith, are careless, reckless, or result from wilful ignorance of facts that could have been ascertained with reasonable diligence — such negligent mistakes do not attract the protect...
- Acts done with actual criminal knowledge or criminal intention, where the person was aware of the true factual situation but chose to act anyway, cannot be shielded by pleading a mistake of fact.
- Situations where the erroneous belief is clearly unreasonable or implausible given the circumstances, and no prudent person in that position would have formed such a belief, are generally excluded from the protection...

Define the term 'Notary Public' as used in the Registration Act, 1908.

In plain terms: A Notary Public is an officially appointed legal officer who has the authority to witness, certify, and authenticate important legal documents. Under the Registration Act, when an Indian property owner or party lives outside India and wants to authorise someone else to register documents on their behalf in India, they can sign a power of attorney in front of a Notary Public in the country where they are living. This authenticated document is then accepted by Indian registration offices as valid proof of authority. Legally: A Notary Public, for the purposes of Section 33 of the Registration Act, is an official authority empowered to execute and authenticate a power-of-attorney on behalf of a principal who does not reside in India, such authenticated power-of-attorney being recognised for the purposes of presenting documents for registration under Section 32 of the Act. (Source: Registration Act, 1908, Section 33.)

In plain terms: A 'company' refers to a business entity that has been legally registered and incorporated under company law, such as a private limited company or a public limited company in India. Legally: The term 'company' is not separately defined in Section 2 of this Act, but as used in the Act, 'company' means a company as defined under the Companies Act, and is expressly included as a sub-category of 'person' under Section 2 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. In plain terms: A 'class of citizens' means any group of people who are citizens of India and share a common religion or set of religious beliefs. This could be Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists, or any other religious community within India. Why is the legal definition of 'works first published in India' important under the Copyright Act, 1957?

Whether a work qualifies as 'first published in India' determines whether it is entitled to the full suite of copyright protections under the Act; if it does qualify, copyright subsists in it and infringement provisions, moral rights, and licensing obligations are triggered. Conversely, where the Central Government invokes Section 42 and restricts these provisions for works of foreign nationals whose home country does not protect Indian authors, those works lose copyright protection in India entirely, meaning no infringement action can be brought and no royalties are owed.

Under the Information Technology Act, 2000, what does 'public key' mean?

In plain terms: A public key is one of two mathematically linked keys used in digital signing. While the private key is kept secret by its owner and used to create a digital signature, the public key is shared openly with anyone who needs to verify that the signature is genuine. It works like a publicly available padlock that anyone can check but only the owner's private key can open. Legally: "public key" means the key of a key pair used to verify a digital signature and listed in the Digital Signature Certificate, being the counterpart of the private key in an asymmetric crypto system. (Source: Information Technology Act, 2000, Section 2.)

What is meant by 'presents' in Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, Section 3?

In plain terms: Presents are gifts given freely to either the bride or groom at the time of their wedding, where nobody has demanded those gifts as a condition of the marriage. These gifts are perfectly legal as long as they are written down in a proper official list as required by the law. However, gifts given to the groom from the bride's side must follow local customs and must not be unreasonably expensive compared to what the giver can afford. Legally: Presents, as used in Section 3(2) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, are gifts given voluntarily at the time of a marriage to either the bride or the bridegroom, without any demand having been made in that behalf, and which are required to be entered in a list maintained in accordance with the rules made under this Act; presents given to the bridegroom by or on behalf of the bride or any person related to the bride must additionally be of a customary nature and not of excessive value having regard to the financial status of the giver. (Source: Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, Section 3.)

What is meant by 'knowingly' in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 3?

In plain terms: Acting 'knowingly' means that a person is fully aware of what they are doing and what the likely result will be, yet they still go ahead with the act or fail to act. It is not enough to say 'I did not know' — if the facts show that the person clearly understood the situation, the law treats them as having acted knowingly. This is stronger than being careless (negligent) but may not always require the specific desire to cause harm (intention). Legally: A person acts 'knowingly' when they are aware of a fact or circumstance with certainty or near-certainty, or are conscious that a particular consequence will or is substantially likely to result from their act or omission. It denotes actual subjective awareness of the relevant fact, circumstance, or consequence at the time the act or omission is committed, as distinguished from mere suspicion, negligence, or constructive notice. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 3.)

Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, what does 'specified by regulations' mean?

In plain terms: When the law says something is 'specified by regulations,' it means the exact details or rules on that particular matter will be written out separately by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) in official regulations, not in the main law itself. What is expressly NOT covered by the term 'instrumentality of State' under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023?

'instrumentality of State' under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 does NOT cover:
- Private companies, corporations, or individuals even if they contract with or provide services to the government — they are not instrumentalities of State and cannot claim this exemption.
- Government-owned commercial enterprises or public sector undertakings (PSUs) functioning primarily for commercial purposes, unless specifically notified by the Central Government under Section 17(2)(a).
- Courts, tribunals, and quasi-judicial bodies, which have a separate and distinct exemption under Section 17(1)(b) and are not covered under the instrumentality of State provision.
- Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) or autonomous bodies that receive government funding but do not exercise sovereign or governmental functions and have not been notified by the Central Government.

Define the term 'endorsement' as used in the Registration Act, 1908.

In plain terms: An endorsement is a written note or entry made by an official registration officer on a separate slip or sheet attached to or covering a document that has been submitted for registration. It is the registering officer's official written mark or record placed on the document or its accompanying slip during the registration process. This endorsement forms part of the official registration record. Legally: "Endorsement" and "endorsed" include and apply to an entry in writing by a registering officer on a rider or covering slip to any document tendered for registration under this Act. (Source: Registration Act, 1908, Section 2.)

What is expressly NOT covered by the term 'residues of veterinary drugs' under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006?

Why is the legal definition of 'musical work' important under the Copyright Act, 1957?

Whether a creation qualifies as a 'musical work' directly determines who holds authorship (the composer), the duration of copyright protection (lifetime plus sixty years), and what acts constitute infringement — including unauthorised reproduction, public performance, broadcasting, or making cover versions under Section 31C. The length of an employee's continuous employment directly determines the minimum statutory notice period the employer must give before terminating a contract of unspecified duration under Section 91, with thresholds at six months, two years, and six years triggering progressively longer notice obligations ranging from one day to two months. Why is the legal definition of 'riot' important under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?

Whether an incident qualifies as a riot determines collective criminal liability — all members of the unlawful assembly face punishment of up to two years (or up to five years if armed), even without personally using force. Under the Information Technology Act, 2000, what does 'cognizable' mean?

In plain terms: A 'cognizable' offence is one serious enough that the police can arrest the accused person immediately without needing to get permission from a court first. Under the IT Act, any offence that carries a punishment of three years or more in jail is treated as cognizable. This means police have stronger powers to act quickly — they can arrest, search, and investigate without waiting for a warrant. Legally: An offence is 'cognizable' under the Information Technology Act, 2000 if it is punishable with imprisonment of three years and above, as provided under Section 77B, which states that such offences shall be cognizable notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. A cognizable offence is one in which a police officer may arrest a person without a warrant, investigate, and take other actions without prior permission of a Magistrate. (Source: Information Technology Act, 2000, Section 77B.)

Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, what does 'misconception of fact' mean?

In plain terms: A 'misconception of fact' means that a person agreed to something based on a false or incorrect belief about a real-world fact. For example, if someone is tricked into thinking they are doing one thing when they are actually doing something completely different, their agreement does not count as real consent. The law says that if the person who benefits from that agreement knew the other person had the wrong idea, the consent is invalid. Legally: A misconception of fact, within the meaning of Section 28, refers to a false belief held by a consenting person regarding a material fact, where such belief is not true, and where the person doing the act knows or has reason to believe that the consent was given in consequence of such misconception. Consent so obtained does not constitute valid consent under this Sanhita. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 28.)

Under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, what does 'criminal misconduct' mean?

In plain terms: Criminal misconduct means when a government official either steals or misuses public money or property in their care, or becomes richer than their legitimate salary and income can explain. If a public servant has assets or cash far beyond what their official income allows, the law presumes they acquired it through corrupt means. This is one of the most serious corruption offences a government employee can commit in India. Legally: A public servant is said to commit the offence of criminal misconduct if he dishonestly or fraudulently misappropriates or otherwise converts for his own use any property entrusted to him or any property under his control as a public servant or allows any other person so to do; or if he intentionally enriches himself illicitly during the period of his office, including by being in possession of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income which he cannot satisfactorily account for. (Source: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, Section 13.)

What is meant by 'consent' in Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Section 3?

In plain terms: Consent means that a person freely and willingly agreed to something being done to them, without any force, threat, or fear. If someone agrees only because they were threatened with death or serious harm to themselves or someone they care about, that agreement does not count as real consent. Under this law, doing something to a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe person without their genuine consent, or by tricking them through fear, is treated as a serious criminal offence. Legally: Consent, as used in the Act, means voluntary and uncoerced agreement by a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe to an act done against or upon their person; consent obtained by putting the person, or any other person in whom the person is interested, in fear of death or of hurt does not constitute valid consent. An act done without the person's consent, against the person's will, or under coerced consent amounts to an aggravated offence under Section 3. (Source: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Section 3.)

Under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, what does 'transfer' mean?

In plain terms: Transfer means any act by which a person moves, hands over, converts, or otherwise deals with property that was obtained through drug-related crimes. This includes selling, gifting, mortgaging, leasing, assigning, or settling such property into a trust. The purpose behind making such a transfer — especially to hide where the money or property came from — is what makes it illegal under the NDPS Act. Legally: 'Transfer' in the context of Chapter VA of the NDPS Act means any act of converting, transferring, or otherwise dealing with property derived from an offence under the Act, including for the purpose of concealing or disguising the illicit origin of such property or to assist any person in evading the legal consequences of such offence. Under Section 68M, 'transfer' encompasses any disposition, conveyance, assignment, settlement, delivery, payment, or other alienation of property, including the creation of a trust or the grant of any lease, mortgage, charge, or other security. (Source: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 68M.)

Define the term 'justified by law' as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

In plain terms: An action is 'justified by law' when the law itself gives a person the right or authority to do it, making it perfectly legal. Even if the person is factually mistaken about the situation but genuinely and honestly believed the law permitted the action, they are still protected from criminal liability. However, being wrong about what the law says (as opposed to being wrong about the facts) does not provide this protection. Legally: An act is 'justified by law' when it is expressly or impliedly authorised or sanctioned by law, such that the person performing it incurs no criminal liability; and by extension under Section 17, a person who by reason of a mistake of fact (and not a mistake of law) in good faith believes himself to be so justified is equally protected, provided the act done falls within the scope of such believed legal authority. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 17.)

What is meant by 'notified area' in Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, Section 100?

In plain terms: A 'notified area' is a geographic area officially declared by a State Government in the Official Gazette where a State-run transport service (like a State Road Transport Corporation) has been given exclusive or priority rights to operate buses or other vehicles. Once an area is declared 'notified,' private bus or vehicle operators face strict restrictions on running their services there. Essentially, it is a government-controlled zone for public road transport. Legally: The area to which an approved scheme relates, being the area covered by a scheme published in the Official Gazette by the State Government under sub-section (3) of section 100, upon which publication such scheme becomes final; the area is so designated upon the approved scheme coming into force and is subject to exclusive or preferential operation by the State transport undertaking. (Source: Arms Act, 1959, Section 18.)

What is expressly NOT covered by the term 'imprisonment for life' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?

'imprisonment for life' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 does NOT cover:
- Simple imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment for a fixed number of years, which are distinct descriptions of imprisonment under Section 4 and do not constitute imprisonment for life.
- The death penalty, which is a separate and superior punishment listed under Section 4 and is not subsumed within or interchangeable with imprisonment for life.
- Community service, fine, and forfeiture of property, which are entirely different categories of punishment under Section 4 and have no connection to imprisonment for life.
- Imprisonment for a definite term — even if it is the maximum of 10 or 14 years — which remains a fixed-term sentence and is legally distinct from imprisonment for life.

Under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, what does 'opium derivative' mean?

In plain terms: Opium derivatives are substances chemically made from opium, including powerful drugs like morphine and heroin, as well as their salts and any medicine or preparation that contains more than a small specified amount of morphine. In simple terms, these are processed or chemically altered forms of opium that are tightly controlled because of their high potential for abuse and addiction. The government can also add new opium-based substances to this category through an official notification. Legally: "opium derivative" means morphine, that is, the principal alkaloid of opium and the salts of morphine; diacetylmorphine, that is, the alkaloid also known as diamorphine or heroin and the salts of diacetylmorphine; all preparations containing more than 0.2 per cent. of morphine or containing any diacetylmorphine; and includes any other derivative of opium or preparation thereof which the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be an opium derivative. (Source: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 2.)

What is meant by 'performing rights society' in Copyright Act, 1957, Section 33?

In plain terms: A performing rights society is an organisation that existed before 1994 and was already in the business of giving out licences for the use of copyrighted works — such as music or performances — on behalf of copyright owners. After the 1994 amendment to the Copyright Act, such societies were automatically treated as copyright societies and were required to re-register within one year. Essentially, it is the predecessor form of what is now called a 'copyright society' under Indian law. Legally: A performing rights society means an association of persons that was functioning in the business of issuing or granting licences in respect of any work in which copyright subsists or in respect of any other rights conferred by this Act, in accordance with the provisions of section 33 on the date immediately before the coming into force of the Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994 (38 of 1994), and which is deemed to be a copyright society for the purposes of Chapter VII upon such commencement. (Source: Copyright Act, 1957, Section 33.)

Under the Code on Wages, 2019 / Labour Codes, what does 'works committee' mean?

In plain terms: A Works Committee is a group of workers elected by employees at a workplace to represent them in discussions with management. It is set up when a trade union requests it at a workplace with 50 or more employees. The committee must be consulted by the employer on important matters like planned dismissals or restructuring, giving workers a formal voice in major decisions affecting their jobs. Legally: A Works Committee is a body comprising employees of an establishment, elected by secret ballot at intervals determined by the employer (but at least once every three years), established at the request of a trade union where an employer employs fifty or more employees at a single establishment for a continuous period of three months, for the purpose of consultation on matters including redundancy and reorganisation. (Source: Code on Wages, 2019 / Labour Codes, Section 165.)

Define the term 'digital signature' as used in the Information Technology Act, 2000.

In plain terms: A digital signature is a secure, electronic way for a person to sign or authenticate a digital document, similar to a handwritten signature but done using a specific technology described in Section 3 of the IT Act. It verifies that the document was signed by a specific person and that the content has not been altered after signing. In India, it is legally recognised and carries the same weight as a physical signature for most official and commercial purposes. Legally: "digital signature" means authentication of any electronic record by a subscriber by means of an electronic method or procedure in accordance with the provisions of section 3. (Source: Information Technology Act, 2000, Section 2.)

What is meant by 'pornographic' in Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, Section 11?

In plain terms: The word 'pornographic' refers to anything related to creating, showing, or using sexual content that involves a child. This includes showing a child sexually explicit objects or images, or trying to involve a child in sexual content for someone else's gratification. Under this law, even the intent to use something pornographic against a child is enough to be considered an offence. Legally: The term 'pornographic' is not separately defined in the Act but is used contextually to describe content, purposes, or acts involving the sexual exploitation or indecent representation of a child through any form of media, including showing objects to a child for pornographic purposes or enticing a child for pornographic purposes, as used in Section 11. It encompasses any material, act, or intent directed at the sexual gratification of a person through the depiction or involvement of a child. (Source: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, Section 11.)

Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, what does 'proceeds of crime' mean?

In plain terms: Proceeds of crime means any money, property, or assets that a person gains as a result of committing organised crime — such as money earned from drug trafficking, extortion, or kidnapping. It covers both directly obtained benefits (like ransom money) and indirectly derived gains (like property bought using crime money). Essentially, it is the profit or benefit that comes out of criminal activity carried out by organised criminal groups. Legally: Proceeds of crime, as used in Section 111 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to any property, whether movable or immovable, that has been derived, obtained, or acquired through the commission of an organised crime or any continuing unlawful activity undertaken by a member of, or on behalf of, an organised crime syndicate, including the direct or indirect material or financial benefits flowing from such criminal activity. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 111.)

What is meant by 'transferee in good faith' in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 68A?

In plain terms: A transferee in good faith is someone who bought or received property honestly, paying a fair price, without knowing (and without any reasonable way of knowing) that the property originally came from drug trafficking or other NDPS offences. Such a person is protected from having that property seized or forfeited under the law. In simple terms, it is an innocent buyer who had no idea about the illegal origins of what they purchased. Legally: A 'transferee in good faith' is a person who has acquired property for adequate consideration without knowledge or reasonable means of knowledge that the property was illegally acquired or traceable to illicit traffic in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, such that the acquisition is honest and without any intent to defeat the provisions of Chapter VA of the NDPS Act. (Source: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 68A.)

Define the term 'commute' as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

In plain terms: Commuting a sentence means officially changing a criminal's punishment to a different, usually less severe, form of punishment. This is done by the government — either Central or State — depending on the type of offence, and the prisoner's agreement is not needed. For example, a death sentence could be commuted to life imprisonment. Legally: To commute, in the context of Section 5 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, means the act by which the appropriate Government substitutes a punishment awarded under this Sanhita with a lesser or different punishment, without requiring the consent of the offender, in accordance with section 474 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 5.)

In plain terms: Subsidiary legislation refers to rules, regulations, and orders that government ministers or officials create under the powers given to them by the main Act, rather than laws directly passed by Parliament. Think of it as the detailed rulebook that fills in the specifics of how the broader law is to be followed in practice. For example, the main Act may say workplaces must be safe, and subsidiary legislation would spell out exactly what safety standards must be met and how. Legally: Subsidiary legislation means any regulation, order, rule, or other legislative instrument made under the authority of this Act by the Minister or other competent authority, and includes regulations prescribing standards and methods for compliance with obligations under this Act, as well as orders requiring employers or operators of workplaces to take specified safety, health, or welfare measures. (Source: Code on Wages, 2019 / Labour Codes, Section 119.)

What is meant by 'false complaint' in Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, Section 22?

In plain terms: A false complaint means when someone knowingly lies about another person committing a child sexual abuse offence under this law, and their only reason for doing so is to harm that person's reputation, force money from them, or intimidate them. It is treated as a serious wrong under this law. However, if the person making the false complaint is a child, they cannot be punished for it. Legally: A false complaint is a complaint made against any person in respect of an offence under sections 3, 5, 7, or 9 of this Act, which is knowingly untrue and made solely with the intention to humiliate, extort, threaten, or defame the accused person. Where such a false complaint is made by a person who is not a child against a child, knowing it to be false, it constitutes an aggravated form that victimizes the child. (Source: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, Section 22.)

What is meant by 'Joint Industrial Council Agreement' in Code on Wages, 2019 / Labour Codes, Section 110?

In plain terms: A Joint Industrial Council Agreement is a formal written deal made by a body representing both employers and workers' unions that sets the minimum standards for employment — such as sick leave, wages, and working conditions — in a particular industry or job type. Once officially published, these standards automatically become part of every qualifying worker's employment contract. Any existing contract terms that offer less than these standards become void. Legally: A 'Joint Industrial Council Agreement' means an agreement made by the Joint Industrial Council, by majority agreement of representatives of employers and trade unions, fixing or revising minimum terms and conditions of employment for employees or categories of employees within specified industries or job categories, which upon publication becomes implied into each covered employee's contract of employment and supersedes any less favourable contractual provision. (Source: Code on Wages, 2019 / Labour Codes, Section 110.)

What is expressly NOT covered by the term 'work' under the Copyright Act, 1957?

'work' under the Copyright Act, 1957 does NOT cover:
- Mere ideas, concepts, themes, plots, or principles that have not been expressed or fixed in a tangible form — copyright protects expression, not the underlying idea.
- News of the day and other miscellaneous facts having the character of mere items of press information, which are explicitly excluded from copyright protection.
- Works not falling into the six enumerated categories (literary, dramatic, musical, artistic, cinematograph film, sound recording), such as a purely functional industrial design not possessing artistic character.
- Performances or broadcasts in themselves, which are protected separately as neighbouring rights (performer's right, broadcast reproduction right) and are not 'works' in the copyright sense.

Define the term 'women's or children's institution' as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

In plain terms: A women's or children's institution is any place—regardless of what it is officially called—that is set up and run specifically to shelter, house, or take care of women or children. This includes orphanages, widow homes, and homes for neglected women or children. The name or label given to such a place does not matter; what matters is that its purpose is the reception and care of women or children. Legally: "Women's or children's institution" means an institution, whether called an orphanage or a home for neglected women or children or a widow's home or an institution called by any other name, which is established and maintained for the reception and care of women or children. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 64.)

Under the Copyright Act, 1957, what does 'domiciled' mean?

In plain terms: Being 'domiciled' in a country means that a person has made that country their permanent home or place of settled residence. For an individual author, domicile is assessed during the period when the work was being created. For companies and other corporate bodies, they are treated as domiciled in India if they were registered or incorporated under Indian law. Legally: An author of a work shall be deemed to be domiciled in a country if, during any substantial part of the period over which the making of an unpublished work is extended, the author was domiciled in that country. For the purposes of this Act, a body corporate shall be deemed to be domiciled in India if it is incorporated under any law in force in India. (Source: Copyright Act, 1957, Section 7.)

What is expressly NOT covered by the term 'public nuisance' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?

'public nuisance' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 does NOT cover:
- Private nuisances that affect only one individual or a very limited group of identified persons, as opposed to the public or a general class of persons in the vicinity.

- Acts that cause harm exclusively within private premises without any spillover effect on the public, neighbouring residents, or users of public rights.

Define the term 'State prisoner' as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

In plain terms: A State prisoner is someone who is locked up by the government not because they committed an ordinary crime, but for political or national security reasons — for example, someone considered a threat to the stability or safety of the country. They are held under special government orders rather than through the regular criminal court process. Because of the sensitive nature of their detention, the law treats any escape or assistance in escaping very seriously. Legally: A 'State prisoner' is a person confined by order of the Government on grounds of State security, political reasons, or reasons of State policy, as distinguished from a person confined under the ordinary criminal law. Such a prisoner is held in lawful custody and their escape, whether facilitated voluntarily or negligently by a public servant, or aided by any person, constitutes a distinct category of offence under this Sanhita. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 156.)

Under the Copyright Act, 1957, what does 'video film' mean?

In plain terms: A video film is a recorded moving image production — like a movie, documentary, or TV serial — that is captured and stored on video format (such as VHS, DVD, digital file, etc.) rather than traditional celluloid film. It works just like a cinema film but uses video technology to record and play back visuals, usually accompanied by sound. Under Indian copyright law, it is treated as part of the broader category of cinematograph films and enjoys the same legal protections. Legally: Video film is included within the definition of 'cinematograph film' under Section 2(f) of the Copyright Act, 1957, which defines 'cinematograph film' as any work of visual recording and includes a sound recording accompanying such visual recording; 'cinematograph' is construed as including any work produced by any process analogous to cinematography including video films. Though not separately defined, a video film is a work of visual recording produced by a process analogous to cinematography, recorded and reproduced on a video medium. (Source: Copyright Act, 1957, Section 2.)

Under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, what does 'member' mean?

In plain terms: A 'member' is a person officially appointed by the State Government to sit on a State or Regional Transport Authority — a body that regulates road transport permits and related matters. These members can be government officials or private individuals, but they must not have any financial stake in any transport business. If a member later acquires such a financial interest, they must disclose it and resign from the Authority. Legally: A member of a State Transport Authority or Regional Transport Authority means any person (whether official or non-official) appointed by the State Government to constitute such Authority under Section 68, excluding any person who has any financial interest, whether as proprietor, employee or otherwise, in any transport undertaking; and in the case of a Regional Transport Authority, not more than two such other persons, and in the case of a State Transport Authority, not more than four such other persons, in addition to the Chairman. (Source: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, Section 68.)

Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, what does 'fabricated evidence' mean?

In plain terms: Fabricated evidence means any proof or material — such as documents, witness statements, or physical objects — that has been made up, forged, or dishonestly altered to mislead a court or official proceeding. It is evidence that the person using or creating it knows is not genuine or truthful. In simple terms, it is 'planted' or 'manufactured' proof intended to deceive a judge or investigating authority. Legally: Evidence that has been manufactured, invented, or altered so as to be false, and which did not genuinely arise from or correspond to actual facts or events; evidence is 'fabricated' within the meaning of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 when it is created or tampered with to produce a false belief in a court or authority as to a matter of fact, as contemplated by Sections 227–233 governing false and fabricated evidence. (Source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Section 233.)

What is expressly NOT covered by the term 'false document' under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988?

'false document' under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 does NOT cover:
- A genuine document that has simply expired — an expired licence or permit is not a false document; it remains an authentic document that is no longer valid.

- A duplicate copy of a legitimately issued document obtained through proper channels from the licensing or registering authority, even if the original also exists.
- A document belonging to a different vehicle or person that is accidentally carried without any fraudulent intent, as intent to deceive is a necessary element under Section 464 IPC.

Define the term 'foster care' as used in the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015.

In plain terms: Foster care is when a child who cannot live with their own family is placed by a government authority with another family, called a foster family, to live with and be cared for temporarily or for a longer period. This is different from adoption because the child does not become a permanent legal member of the foster family. The arrangement is overseen and regulated by child welfare authorities to ensure the child's safety and well-being. Legally: Foster care means a form of alternative care where a child in need of care and protection is placed by the Committee with a foster family that is registered with the District Child Protection Unit, to provide a family-based care arrangement for the child on a temporary or long-term basis, as an alternative to institutional care. (Source: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, Section 2.)

Why is the legal definition of 'dangerous driving' important under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988?

Whether conduct qualifies as dangerous driving under Section 184 directly triggers the automatic suspension of the accused's driving licence under Section 21 upon registration of a police case, and empowers the court to cancel or suspend the licence upon conviction under Section 22. Define the term 'provident fund' as used in the Payment of Wages Act, 1936.

In plain terms: A provident fund is a savings and retirement scheme where both the employer and the employee contribute a portion of the employee's salary regularly. The money accumulates over time and is paid out to the employee upon retirement, resignation, or in certain emergencies. Under the Payment of Wages Act, deductions from wages for contributions to a provident fund are permitted by law, and the employer's own contributions to such a fund are not counted as part of the employee's wages. Legally: The term 'provident fund' is not formally defined in the Payment of Wages Act, but as used in Section 7(2) and Section 2, it refers to a statutory or contractual fund to which an employer makes contributions on behalf of an employed person, and from which deductions from wages may be lawfully made; any such contribution paid by the employer to a provident fund, and the interest accrued thereon, is expressly excluded from the definition of 'wages' under Section 2. (Source: Payment of Wages Act, 1936, Section 7.)

- Acts committed entirely outside India that have no connection to India and do not involve Indian nationals or Indian territory at any stage.
